hints: Think about which groups contain acidic $O-H$ bonds that can release $H_2$ with $Na$ or $CO_2$ with $Na_2CO_3$, and why carbonate needs a stronger acid.
Recall which functional group forms an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH and which subgroup within it also reduces Fehling's reagent on warming.
Remember the iodoform test with $I_2(aq) + OH^-(aq)$ needs a specific $CH_3CO$ or $CH_3CH(OH)$ unit, not just any carbonyl or alcohol.
Consider which unsaturated functional group decolourises $Br_2(aq)$ by electrophilic addition, with no oxygen needed.
walkthrough:
Separate the acidic $O-H$ tests**
Picture $Na$ as a very strong base that will take $H^+$ even from a weak acid. Both $R-OH$ and $R-COOH$ give $H_2$ effervescence, so sodium metal is positive for alcohol or carboxylic acid. $Na_2CO_3(aq)$ is much more selective. Only a strong enough organic acid to protonate carbonate to $CO_2$, that is a carboxylic acid, gives effervescence. Phenols and alcohols are not acidic enough.

Pin down the carbonyl tests**
2,4-DNPH is your general carbonyl detector. Both aldehydes and ketones do nucleophilic addition-elimination to give the orange precipitate. Fehling's reagent then splits them. Only aldehydes, $R-CHO$, are easily oxidised on warming to give the brick-red $Cu_2O$ precipitate. Ketones stay blue.

Remember the iodoform structural requirement**
The $I_2$ in $NaOH$ test is not for all carbonyls. You need the $CH_3C=O$ group in a methyl ketone, or the oxidisable $CH_3CH(OH)$ group in a methyl secondary alcohol which is oxidised in situ to the methyl ketone, to form yellow $CHI_3$. So write methyl ketone (methyl alcohol with that unit also accepted).

Spot the alkene test**
$Br_2(aq)$ from orange to colourless is electrophilic addition across $C=C$. In aliphatic compounds this means alkene. No other group in this list decolourises bromine water.

Final answer: sodium metal: alcohol or carboxylic acid; $Na_2CO_3(aq)$: carboxylic acid; 2,4-DNPH: aldehyde or ketone (carbonyl); $I_2(aq) + OH^-(aq)$: methyl ketone (or methyl secondary alcohol with $CH_3CH(OH)$ group); warm with Fehling's: aldehyde; $Br_2(aq)$: alkene.

hints: Compare $A$ ($C_{10}H_{18}O$) to $B$ ($C_{10}H_{16}O$) for loss of $H_2$, then use the fact $B$ gives a positive Fehling test to work back to what $A$ must be.
walkthrough:
Read the formulae and the Fehling clue together**
$A$ is $C_{10}H_{18}O$ and $B$ is $C_{10}H_{16}O$. That is a loss of $H_2$, classic for alcohol to carbonyl oxidation. Now $B$ is positive with Fehling's, so $B$ must be an aldehyde, $R-CHO$. The only alcohol that oxidises to an aldehyde is a primary alcohol, $R-CH_2OH$. A secondary alcohol would give a ketone which is Fehling negative.
Final answer: (primary) alcohol, as $A$ loses $H_2$ to form $B$ which is an aldehyde (positive Fehling's).

hints: Look at $A$ ($C_{10}H_{18}O$) to $B$ ($C_{10}H_{16}O$) as loss of hydrogen and link to the primary alcohol to aldehyde change.
Look at $C$ ($C_6H_8O_5$) to $E$ ($C_6H_{10}O_5$) with $NaBH_4$ and think what $NaBH_4$ does to a ketone or aldehyde.
Look at $E$ ($C_6H_{10}O_5$) to $F$ ($C_6H_8O_4$) with conc. $H_2SO_4$ and loss of $H_2O$, and recall what conc. acid does to an alcohol.
walkthrough:
Classify $A$ to $B$**
You go from $CH_2OH$ to $CHO$. Hydrogen is removed, oxygen ratio increases. That is oxidation. In organic terms it is also dehydrogenation. No water is lost, so it is not dehydration.

Classify $C$ to $E$ with $NaBH_4$**
$NaBH_4$ is a classic hydride reducing agent. It delivers $H^-$ to a $C=O$ in nucleophilic addition, then work up gives $C-OH$. Formula gains $H_2$ from $C_6H_8O_5$ to $C_6H_{10}O_5$. So this is reduction, specifically nucleophilic addition to the ketone in $C$.

Classify $E$ to $F$ with conc. $H_2SO_4$**
Heating an alcohol with concentrated $H_2SO_4$ removes $H_2O$ from adjacent carbons to form $C=C$. Here $C_6H_{10}O_5$ to $C_6H_8O_4$ is loss of $H_2O$. That is elimination, specifically dehydration.
Final answer: $A \rightarrow B$: oxidation (dehydrogenation); $C \rightarrow E$: reduction (nucleophilic addition); $E \rightarrow F$: elimination (dehydration).

hints: Use Table 6.2 for $H$: positive with $Na$ and $Na_2CO_3$ only, formula $C_2H_4O_2$, to identify the simplest familiar acid.
Use Table 6.2 for $G$: acid plus ketone but no iodoform and no alkene, formula $C_4H_4O_5$, and think of $F$ cleaved at $C=C$ to give $H$ plus $G$.
walkthrough:
Solve $H$ first as the anchor**
$H$ is $C_2H_4O_2$ and is positive only with sodium and carbonate. That screams carboxylic acid with no other reactive group. No DNPH, no iodoform, no Fehling, no bromine. The only $C_2$ acid is ethanoic acid, $CH_3COOH$. This fits perfectly.

Reconstruct $G$ from cleavage logic**
$F$ ($C_6H_8O_4$) is cleaved by hot acidified $KMnO_4$ at its $C=C$ to $G$ ($C_4H_4O_5$) + $H$ ($C_2H_4O_2$). $G$ is acid positive and DNPH positive, so it has $COOH$ plus ketone or aldehyde, but Fehling negative so no aldehyde, and iodoform negative so no $CH_3CO$ group. With $C_4H_4O_5$ that points to a keto-diacid with no methyl: $HOOC-CH_2-CO-COOH$. Check atoms: $C_4H_4O_5$ matches, and cleavage of $F$ to give $CH_3COOH$ + this keto-diacid balances with oxidising conditions.
Final answer: $G$: $HOOCCH_2COCOOH$, i.e. $HO-C(=O)-CH_2-C(=O)-C(=O)-OH$ (3-oxobutanedioic acid); $H$: $CH_3COOH$, ethanoic acid, i.e. $CH_3-C(=O)-OH$.

hints: Start from $D$ ($C_3H_6O$) which is DNPH and iodoform positive but Fehling negative, to identify the only $C_3$ methyl ketone.
Work backwards from $G$ + $H$ to $F$ by joining the cleavage ends with a $C=C$ bond, using the fact $F$ is a diacid alkene with no ketone.
Convert the $C=C$ in $F$ back to $C(OH)-CH$ in $E$ and the $CH(OH)$ in $E$ back to $C=O$ in $C$, keeping the two $COOH$ groups untouched.
Use atom balance $A$ ($C_{10}H_{18}O$) to $C$ ($C_6H_8O_5$) + $D$ ($C_3H_6O$) + $CO_2$ to place the cleavage points and the primary $CH_2OH$ in $A$.
Check $A$ has two $C=C$ bonds (Br2 positive, formula) and $B$ is the corresponding aldehyde, with $C$ containing a $CH_3CO$ unit for its iodoform test.
walkthrough:
Nail $D$ from its tests**
$D$ is $C_3H_6O$, DNPH positive so carbonyl, iodoform positive so $CH_3CO$, Fehling negative so not aldehyde. That leaves only propanone, $CH_3-C(=O)-CH_3$. No $O-H$, no $C=C$, matching its Table 6.2 row.

Build $F$ by reversing the cleavage**
$F$ ($C_6H_8O_4$) gives $G$ ($HOOC-CH_2-CO-COOH$) + $H$ ($CH_3-COOH$) on vigorous oxidation. That is cleavage of a $C=C$. Join $HOOC-CH_2-C(COOH)=$ to $=CH-CH_3$. You get $HOOC-CH_2-C(COOH)=CH-CH_3$. Check: diacid, alkene positive with $Br_2$, no carbonyl so DNPH negative, formula $C_6H_8O_4$ fits. Perfect.

Step back to $E$ then $C$**
$E$ is $F$ plus $H_2O$ across the double bond. The $OH$ must go on the carbon that becomes $C=O$ in $C$. So $E$ is $HOOC-CH_2-CH(COOH)-CH(OH)-CH_3$. This is a hydroxy-diacid, so acid positive, iodoform positive because of $CH_3CH(OH)$, DNPH negative, matching Table 6.2. Oxidise that secondary alcohol back with $NaBH_4$ in reverse and $C$ is $HOOC-CH_2-CH(COOH)-CO-CH_3$. This restores the methyl ketone, so $C$ is DNPH and iodoform positive, acid positive, alkene negative, as observed.

Reconstruct $A$ and $B$ from the first cleavage**
Hot $KMnO_4$ splits $A$ ($C_{10}H_{18}O$) into $C$ ($C_6$) + $D$ ($C_3$) + $CO_2$ ($C_1$). That accounts for all 10 carbons. $A$ is a primary alcohol diene: $Br_2$ positive, $Na$ positive, no acid, no carbonyl. $B$ is the same skeleton with $CH_2OH$ oxidised to $CHO$, so $B$ is an aldehyde diene, Fehling and DNPH positive. Placing the two $C=C$ bonds so that cleavage gives the $C_6$ keto-diacid plus propanone plus $CO_2$ gives lavandulol, $HOCH_2-CH-C(CH_3)-CH_2-CH=C(CH_3)_2$ with the appropriate double bond positions.

Final answer: $D$: $CH_3COCH_3$, propanone; $F$: $HOOCCH_2C(COOH)=CHCH_3$ (2-methylbut-2-ene-1,4-dioic acid skeleton); $E$: $HOOCCH_2CH(COOH)CH(OH)CH_3$; $C$: $HOOCCH_2CH(COOH)COCH_3$; $A$: primary alcohol diene isomer, e.g. $HOCH_2CH_2C(CH_3)=CHCH=C(CH_3)_2$ type (lavandulol: $HOCH_2CHC(CH_3)CH_2CH=C(CH_3)_2$ with second $C=C$ placed to satisfy cleavage to $C$ + $D$ + $CO_2$).
